Lecture 12: RNLA Case Study

Author

Jamie Haddock

Case study: randomness as a tool for linear algebra

Three randomized algorithms from randomized numerical linear algebra (RNLA):

  1. Randomized Kaczmarz – solve \(Ax=b\) by projecting onto one randomly chosen row at a time.
  2. Randomized trace estimation – estimate \(\mathrm{tr}(A)\) using only products \(z^\top A z\) with a random vector \(z\).
  3. Randomized matrix multiplication – approximate \(AB\) using a few randomly chosen column/row outer products.
The common story

Each method returns a random answer whose expected value is either the exact, or an improved answer.

Part A: Randomized Kaczmarz

Randomized Kaczmarz (RK) solves a consistent linear system \(Ax=b\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rows \(a_1^\top,\dots,a_m^\top\) and \(x^\star\) denotes a solution. Starting from an initial guess \(x_0\) (for instance \(x_0=0\)), at each iteration \(k\) the algorithm:

  1. Samples a row. Draw a row index \(I_k\in\{1,\dots,m\}\) at random from a fixed PMF \(p=(p_1,\dots,p_m)\), independently of all previous draws (sampling with replacement).
  2. Projects onto that equation. Move the current iterate to the closest point on the hyperplane \(\{x : a_{I_k}^\top x=b_{I_k}\}\): \[ x_{k+1}=x_k+\frac{b_{I_k}-a_{I_k}^\top x_k}{\|a_{I_k}\|^2}\,a_{I_k}. \]

After the \(k\)th step the iterate satisfies equation \(I_k\) exactly, so sampling the same row twice in a row (a collision) makes no progress.

Two standard choices of PMF are the row-norm PMF \(p_i=\|a_i\|^2/\|A\|_F^2\) and the uniform PMF \(p_i=1/m\).

Notation: the Frobenius norm

For a matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with entries \(A_{ij}\) and rows \(a_1^\top,\dots,a_m^\top\), the Frobenius norm is \[ \|A\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}^2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\|a_i\|^2 . \]

Collision probability in randomized Kaczmarz

Suppose two consecutive iterations sample rows \(I_1,I_2\) independently, each \(\sim p\) (with replacement). What’s the probability the algorithm samples the same row twice in a row – a collision?

Theorem: Collision probability

\[P(I_1=I_2) = \sum_{i=1}^m p_i^2.\]

Proof: Condition on \(I_1\), applying the law of total probability with partitioning on the value of \(I_1\): \[P(I_1=I_2) = \sum_{i=1}^m P(I_2=i\mid I_1=i)\,P(I_1=i) = \sum_{i=1}^m P(I_2=i)\,p_i = \sum_{i=1}^m p_i^2,\] using independence of \(I_1,I_2\) for \(P(I_2=i\mid I_1=i)=P(I_2=i)=p_i\). \(\blacksquare\)

Why we care: if row \(i\) is sampled twice in a row, the second projection doesn’t update the iterate – the iterate already satisfies \(a_i^\top x=b_i\) exactly after the first projection, so the second step makes zero progress toward \(x^\star\). A high collision probability means wasted iterations.

Fact

The collision probability \(\sum_i p_i^2\) is minimized by the uniform distribution \(p_i=1/m\) (giving \(\sum_i p_i^2=1/m\), the smallest possible value: \(1=(\sum_i p_i)^2 \le m\sum_i p_i^2\) by Cauchy-Schwarz), and maximized at \(1\) when all the probability mass sits on a single row. So concentrating the sampling distribution on a subset of rows comes at the cost of more wasted iterations.

Exercise 1: Bayes’ rule on collisions

Sample \(I_1,I_2\) independently from a PMF \(p\) on \(\{1,\dots,m\}\), and let \(C=\{I_1=I_2\}\) be the collision event.

  1. Use Bayes’ rule and the collision theorem to show that \[P(I_1=i\mid C)=\frac{p_i^2}{\sum_{j=1}^m p_j^2}.\]

  2. Now take \(m=3\) and \(p=(\tfrac12,\tfrac13,\tfrac16)\). Compute \(P(C)\), and compute \(P(I_1=i\mid C)\) for \(i=1,2,3\). Compare each with the unconditional probability \(P(I_1=i)=p_i\). For which rows is the conditional probability larger, and for which is it smaller? Explain in words why a collision makes the heavily weighted row even more likely.

LOTUS: why the row-norm PMF?

A popular distribution over the rows is the row-norm PMF \(p_I(i) = \|a_i\|^2/\|A\|_F^2\). We’ll see why now!

Fix the current iterate \(x_k\) and let \(v = x_k - x^\star\). LOTUS lets us compute the expected value of any function of \(I\) straight from \(p_I\) – for instance \[ E\!\left[\frac{(a_I^\top v)^2}{\|a_I\|^2}\right] = \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{(a_i^\top v)^2}{\|a_i\|^2}\, p_I(i). \]

Plugging in \(p_I(i) = \|a_i\|^2/\|A\|_F^2\), the \(\|a_i\|^2\) cancels: \[ \sum_{i=1}^m \frac{(a_i^\top v)^2}{\|a_i\|^2}\cdot\frac{\|a_i\|^2}{\|A\|_F^2} = \frac{1}{\|A\|_F^2}\sum_{i=1}^m (a_i^\top v)^2 = \frac{\|Av\|^2}{\|A\|_F^2}. \]

If \(I\) were sampled uniformly instead, the \(\|a_i\|^2\) would not cancel, and the final form wouldn’t be so nice and simple!

Linearity + LOTUS: average one-step progress of RK

Recall randomized Kaczmarz’s update, and note that the Pythagorean theorem (the update is an orthogonal projection) provides, \[ \|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|^2 = \|v\|^2 - \frac{(a_I^\top v)^2}{\|a_I\|^2}. \] where \(v = x_k-x^\star\).

\(\|v\|^2\) is a constant given \(x_k\) – only \(I\) is random. By linearity, \[ E\big[\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|^2\big] = \|v\|^2 - E\!\left[\frac{(a_I^\top v)^2}{\|a_I\|^2}\right] = \|v\|^2 - \frac{\|Av\|^2}{\|A\|_F^2}, \] reusing the LOTUS computation from the previous slide!

Since \(\|Av\| \ge \sigma_{\min}(A)\|v\|\), \[ E\big[\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|^2\big] \;\le\; \left(1 - \frac{\sigma_{\min}(A)^2}{\|A\|_F^2}\right)\|x_k-x^\star\|^2. \] Every step shrinks the expected squared error by a fixed factor – this a very nice (and very well-cited) result from Thomas Strohmer and Roman Vershynin in 2009!

Watching the bound play out over many steps

The one-step bound says the expected squared error shrinks by a fixed factor every step. Let’s actually run RK and watch \(\|x_k-x^\star\|^2\) decrease and compare it to the bound.

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(151)
m, n = 20, 8
A = rng.standard_normal((m, n))
x_star = rng.standard_normal(n)
b = A @ x_star
row_norm_sq = (A ** 2).sum(axis=1)
p_row_norm = row_norm_sq / row_norm_sq.sum()
sigma_min = np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)[-1]
frob_sq = row_norm_sq.sum()

num_steps = 60
num_runs = 300
errors_sq = np.zeros((num_runs, num_steps + 1))

for r in range(num_runs):
    x = np.zeros(n)
    errors_sq[r, 0] = np.linalg.norm(x - x_star) ** 2
    idx_sequence = rng.choice(m, size=num_steps, p=p_row_norm)
    for t, i in enumerate(idx_sequence, start=1):
        a_i, b_i = A[i], b[i]
        x = x + (b_i - a_i @ x) / row_norm_sq[i] * a_i
        errors_sq[r, t] = np.linalg.norm(x - x_star) ** 2

mean_error_sq = errors_sq.mean(axis=0)
bound_curve = errors_sq[:, 0].mean() * (1 - sigma_min**2 / frob_sq) ** np.arange(num_steps + 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.semilogy(mean_error_sq, label="average of $\\|x_k-x^\\star\\|^2$ over runs")
ax.semilogy(bound_curve, "--", label="one-step bound, applied repeatedly")
ax.set_xlabel("step $k$")
ax.set_ylabel("squared error (log scale)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Recursing the randomized Kaczmarz bound

Recall our previous one-step bound, valid conditional on the current iterate \(x_k\): \[ E\big[\|x_{k+1}-x^\star\|^2 \mid x_k\big] \le (1-c)\,\|x_k-x^\star\|^2, \qquad c = \frac{\sigma_{\min}(A)^2}{\|A\|_F^2}. \]

That’s only a statement about one step, conditional on where we happen to be. To turn it into an unconditional guarantee after \(k\) steps, apply the law of iterated expectation repeatedly: \[ \begin{aligned} E\big[\|x_2-x^\star\|^2\big] &= E\Big[E\big[\|x_2-x^\star\|^2 \mid x_1\big]\Big] \le E\big[(1-c)\|x_1-x^\star\|^2\big] \\&= (1-c)\,E\big[\|x_1-x^\star\|^2\big] \le (1-c)^2\|x_0-x^\star\|^2. \end{aligned} \]

Repeating this argument (this is called the tower of iterated expectation) gives, for every \(k\), \[ E\big[\|x_k-x^\star\|^2\big] \le (1-c)^k \|x_0-x^\star\|^2, \] – exactly the compounded bound we plotted before. Now we know why “applying the one-step bound repeatedly” is legitimate: it’s the law of total expectation, used \(k\) times.

Uniform vs. row-norm sampling: the distribution controls the rate

One can prove a similar (but worse) bound for the error for uniform sampling. Let’s run both samplers on a matrix whose row norms vary by orders of magnitude, and compare each empirical curve with its bound.

Code 
rng = np.random.default_rng(151)
m, n = 40, 8
A = rng.standard_normal((m, n)) * (10 ** rng.uniform(-1, 1, size=(m, 1)))  # very unequal row norms
x_star = rng.standard_normal(n)
b = A @ x_star
row_norm_sq = (A ** 2).sum(axis=1)
frob_sq = row_norm_sq.sum()
sigma_min = np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False)[-1]

samplers = {
    "row-norm": row_norm_sq / frob_sq,
    "uniform": np.ones(m) / m,
}
rates = {
    "row-norm": sigma_min**2 / frob_sq,
    "uniform": sigma_min**2 / (m * row_norm_sq.max()),
}

num_steps, num_runs = 400, 300
mean_err = {}
for name, p in samplers.items():
    errs = np.zeros((num_runs, num_steps + 1))
    for r in range(num_runs):
        x = np.zeros(n)
        errs[r, 0] = np.linalg.norm(x - x_star) ** 2
        for t, i in enumerate(rng.choice(m, size=num_steps, p=p), start=1):
            x = x + (b[i] - A[i] @ x) / row_norm_sq[i] * A[i]
            errs[r, t] = np.linalg.norm(x - x_star) ** 2
    mean_err[name] = errs.mean(axis=0)

e0 = np.linalg.norm(x_star) ** 2
ks = np.arange(num_steps + 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
for name, color in [("row-norm", "C0"), ("uniform", "C1")]:
    ax.semilogy(mean_err[name], color=color, label=f"{name}: empirical")
    ax.semilogy(e0 * (1 - rates[name]) ** ks, "--", color=color, label=f"{name}: bound")
ax.set_ylim(1e-20, 1e2)
ax.set_xlabel("step $k$")
ax.set_ylabel("squared error (log scale)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Takeaways
  • The sampling distribution controls the guarantee: row-norm sampling gives a much better bound here.
  • The bounds are only upper bounds. On this matrix uniform sampling actually converges faster in practice – row-norm sampling spends most of its draws on a few huge rows, while uniform sampling touches every row equally often. A bound being better does not mean the algorithm is better on a given matrix.
Exercise 2: distinct rows

Run RK with replacement for \(k\) steps, and let \(D_k\) be the number of distinct rows sampled.

  1. Write \(D_k=\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i\) for indicator RVs \(Y_i\), and say what event \(Y_i\) indicates.

  2. Use independence of the draws to compute \(P(Y_i=1)\), then use linearity to show \[E[D_k]=\sum_{i=1}^m\big(1-(1-p_i)^k\big).\] Check the case \(k=1\).

Part B: Randomized trace estimation

Recall the randomized trace estimator: for \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), draw \(z\in\{-1,+1\}^n\) with i.i.d. Rademacher entries and set \(\tau = z^\top A z = \sum_{i,j} z_iz_j A_{ij}\).

Example: unbiasedness of randomized trace estimation

We’ll now prove \(E[\tau]=\mathrm{tr}(A)\) – recall this is called unbiasedness.

By linearity, \(E[\tau] = \sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\,E[z_iz_j]\). Split into diagonal and off-diagonal terms:

  • Diagonal (\(i=j\)): \(z_i^2=1\) always, so \(E[z_i^2]=1\).
  • Off-diagonal (\(i\ne j\)): \(z_i,z_j\) independent, so by the fact above, \(E[z_iz_j]=E[z_i]E[z_j] = 0\cdot 0=0\) (Rademacher has mean \(0\)).

\[ E[\tau] = \sum_i A_{ii}\cdot 1 + \sum_{i\ne j} A_{ij}\cdot 0 = \sum_i A_{ii} = \mathrm{tr}(A). \]

Exercise 3: breaking the proof

Suppose that instead of independent entries, we use a single random sign \(s\in\{-1,+1\}\) (each with probability \(1/2\)) and set \(z=s\mathbf 1=(s,s,\dots,s)\).

  1. Check that each \(z_i\) still has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\).

  2. Compute \(E[z^\top Az]\). What do you get instead of \(\mathrm{tr}(A)\)?

  3. Which step of the unbiasedness proof fails, and why?

Example: continuous RV in randomized trace estimation

The unbiasedness proof only ever used \[ E[z_i^2] = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad E[z_iz_j] = 0 \ (i\ne j), \] which followed from mean \(0\), variance \(1\), and independence – nothing about \(z_i\) being discrete. So a continuous \(z_i\) works exactly as well.

A continuous alternative

Instead of Rademacher entries \(z_i=\pm1\), draw \(z_i\) i.i.d. from a continuous distribution with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\) – the standard normal \(N(0,1)\) (the Gaussian). The same proof works exactly, just a different distribution!

Code 
rng = np.random.default_rng(151)
d = 50
A = rng.standard_normal((d, d)) + 5 * np.eye(d)
true_trace = np.trace(A)

num_samples = 20_000
Z_rad = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(num_samples, d))  # discrete: Rademacher
Z_gauss = rng.standard_normal((num_samples, d))          # continuous: standard Gaussian

tau_rad = np.einsum('si,ij,sj->s', Z_rad, A, Z_rad)
tau_gauss = np.einsum('si,ij,sj->s', Z_gauss, A, Z_gauss)

print(f"true trace(A)                        = {true_trace:.4f}")
print(f"mean of tau, Rademacher z (discrete)  = {tau_rad.mean():.4f}")
print(f"mean of tau, Gaussian z (continuous)  = {tau_gauss.mean():.4f}")
true trace(A)                        = 250.0783
mean of tau, Rademacher z (discrete)  = 249.9342
mean of tau, Gaussian z (continuous)  = 249.5031

How much variance? The Rademacher estimator

Unbiased is not enough – a single sample of \(\tau\) could be far from \(\mathrm{tr}(A)\). Let \(A\) be symmetric, so \(A_{ij}=A_{ji}\) and \[ \tau=\sum_i A_{ii}z_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}z_iz_j=\mathrm{tr}(A)+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}z_iz_j \] for Rademacher \(z\) (since \(z_i^2=1\)). The first term is a constant, so only the cross terms contribute to the variance.

Variance of the Rademacher estimator. For symmetric \(A\), we have \[ \mathrm{Var}(\tau)=4\,\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\,z_iz_j\Big). \]

Let \(W_{ij}=z_iz_j\) for \(i<j\). We check that these are uncorrelated with variance 1:

  • Mean zero. \(E[W_{ij}]=E[z_i]E[z_j]=0\) by independence.
  • Variance one. \(\mathrm{Var}(W_{ij})=E[z_i^2z_j^2]-0=1\), since \(z_i^2=z_j^2=1\).
  • Pairwise uncorrelated. For distinct pairs \(\{i,j\}\ne\{k,l\}\), the product \(W_{ij}W_{kl}\) has at least one index appearing exactly once. On the other hand, if \(j=k\) then \(W_{ij}W_{jl}=z_iz_j^2z_l=z_iz_l\) with \(i\neq l\). So \(E[W_{ij}W_{kl}]\) is a product of terms including \(E[z_m]=0\), and \(\mathrm{Cov}(W_{ij},W_{kl})=0\).

(They are not mutually independent: \(W_{12}W_{13}W_{23}=1\) always. We only need uncorrelated, since variances add for uncorrelated summands.)

So variances of the sum add: \[ \mathrm{Var}(\tau)=4\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}^2\,\mathrm{Var}(W_{ij})=4\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}^2=2\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}^2, \] where the last step uses \(\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}^2=2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}^2\) by symmetry.

Diagonal matrices

If \(A\) is diagonal, \(\mathrm{Var}(\tau)=0\): every draw of \(z\) gives exactly \(\mathrm{tr}(A)\). The variance only measures the off-diagonal mass.

Exercise 4: variance of the Gaussian estimator

Let \(A\) be symmetric and \(z\) have i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\) entries. You may use \(E[z_i^4]=3\).

  1. Show \(\mathrm{Var}(z_i^2)=2\).

  2. Write \(\tau=\sum_i A_{ii}z_i^2+2\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}z_iz_j\). Argue that all terms are pairwise uncorrelated, and conclude that \[\mathrm{Var}(\tau_{\text{Gauss}})=2\|A\|_F^2.\]

Comparing the two estimators

Since \(\|A\|_F^2=\sum_i A_{ii}^2+\sum_{i\ne j}A_{ij}^2\), the two variances differ by \[ \mathrm{Var}(\tau_{\text{Gauss}})-\mathrm{Var}(\tau_{\text{Rad}})=2\sum_i A_{ii}^2\;\ge 0. \] Rademacher always has smaller variance, and it wins by the most when \(A\) has a heavy diagonal. If \(A\) has zero diagonal, the two are identical. Let’s check on a diagonal-dominant matrix and on one with zero diagonal.

Code 
rng = np.random.default_rng(151)
d = 30
G = rng.standard_normal((d, d))
S = (G + G.T) / 2                                   # symmetric, generic diagonal
A_diag_heavy = S + 5 * np.eye(d)                    # diagonal-dominant
A_zero_diag = S - np.diag(np.diag(S))               # zero diagonal

num_samples = 200_000
for name, M in [("diagonal-dominant", A_diag_heavy), ("zero diagonal", A_zero_diag)]:
    Z_rad = rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(num_samples, d))
    Z_gauss = rng.standard_normal((num_samples, d))
    tau_rad = np.einsum('si,ij,sj->s', Z_rad, M, Z_rad)
    tau_gauss = np.einsum('si,ij,sj->s', Z_gauss, M, Z_gauss)
    off = (M ** 2).sum() - (np.diag(M) ** 2).sum()
    print(name)
    print(f"  Rademacher: empirical var {tau_rad.var():9.2f}   formula {2*off:9.2f}")
    print(f"  Gaussian:   empirical var {tau_gauss.var():9.2f}   formula {2*(M**2).sum():9.2f}")
diagonal-dominant
  Rademacher: empirical var    978.64   formula    983.70
  Gaussian:   empirical var   2578.98   formula   2595.05
zero diagonal
  Rademacher: empirical var    984.84   formula    983.70
  Gaussian:   empirical var    981.17   formula    983.70

Part C: Randomized matrix multiplication

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\). Write \(a_j\) for the \(j\)-th column of \(A\) and \(b_j^\top\) for the \(j\)-th row of \(B\). Then \[ AB=\sum_{j=1}^n a_j b_j^\top, \] a sum of \(n\) rank-one outer products.

Computing all of them is expensive, so sample:

  • draw \(J\sim p\) on \(\{1,\dots,n\}\),
  • form \(X=\dfrac{1}{p_J}\,a_Jb_J^\top\),
  • average \(c\) i.i.d. copies: \(\hat C=\dfrac1c\sum_{t=1}^c X^{(t)}\).

The factor \(1/p_J\) is importance weighting: it compensates for rows that are sampled more often.

Unbiasedness of randomized matrix multiplication

\(X\) is a matrix-valued function \(h(J)\) of the discrete RV \(J\), and by LOTUS: \[ E[X]=\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{p_j}\,a_jb_j^\top\;p_j=\sum_{j=1}^n a_jb_j^\top=AB. \]

By linearity, \(E[\hat C]=\frac1c\sum_t E[X^{(t)}]=AB\) as well.

  • The \(p_j\) cancels – the same cancellation trick as for the row-norm PMF in Kaczmarz.
  • We need \(p_j>0\) wherever \(a_jb_j^\top\ne0\); otherwise those terms are never sampled and the estimator is biased.
  • Unbiasedness holds for every valid \(p\), so the choice of \(p\) will only affect the variance.
(Not on HW) Exercise 5: variance of randomized matrix multiplication

Let \(X=\frac1{p_J}a_Jb_J^\top\) as above, with \(X_{ik}=\frac{a_{ij}b_{jk}}{p_j}\) conditional on \(J=j\) (here \(a_{ij}\) is the \(i\)-th entry of column \(a_j\) and \(b_{jk}\) the \(k\)-th entry of row \(b_j^\top\)).

  1. Use LOTUS and law of total expectation to show \(E[X_{ik}^2]=\sum_{j}\dfrac{a_{ij}^2b_{jk}^2}{p_j}\).

  2. Deduce the variance of the \((i,k)\) entry of the averaged estimator \(\hat C\): \[\mathrm{Var}(\hat C_{ik})=\frac1c\left(\sum_{j}\frac{a_{ij}^2b_{jk}^2}{p_j}-(AB)_{ik}^2\right).\]

The best sampling distribution

Part (b) of the exercise above can be summed to show: \(E\|AB-\hat C\|_F^2=\frac1c\left(\sum_{j}\frac{w_j^2}{p_j}-\|AB\|_F^2\right)\), where \(w_j=\|a_j\|\|b_j\|\). Only the sum depends on \(p\), so minimize \(\sum_j w_j^2/p_j\).

Apply Cauchy-Schwarz, the same trick as in the collision fact: \[ \Big(\sum_j w_j\Big)^2=\Big(\sum_j \tfrac{w_j}{\sqrt{p_j}}\cdot\sqrt{p_j}\Big)^2 \le\Big(\sum_j\tfrac{w_j^2}{p_j}\Big)\Big(\sum_j p_j\Big)=\sum_j\frac{w_j^2}{p_j}. \] Equality holds exactly when \(\frac{w_j}{\sqrt{p_j}}\propto\sqrt{p_j}\), i.e. when \[ \boxed{\,p_j=\frac{\|a_j\|\|b_j\|}{\sum_l\|a_l\|\|b_l\|}\,}, \qquad\text{giving}\qquad E\|AB-\hat C\|_F^2=\frac1c\Big(\big(\textstyle\sum_j w_j\big)^2-\|AB\|_F^2\Big). \]

Compared with uniform sampling

For \(p_j=1/n\) the sum is \(n\sum_j w_j^2\ \ge\ (\sum_j w_j)^2\) (Cauchy-Schwarz again), with equality only when all \(w_j\) are equal. When the \(w_j\) are very unequal, uniform sampling wastes most draws on unimportant terms, and optimal sampling can be far better.

Connection to Kaczmarz. With \(B=A^\top\) we get \(b_j=a_j\), so \(w_j=\|a_j\|^2\) and the optimal PMF is \(p_j\propto\|a_j\|^2\): the same squared-norm weighting as the row-norm PMF in RK. (Here \(a_j\) is a column of \(A\), i.e. a row of \(A^\top\).) In both algorithms, sample in proportion to how much each piece contributes.
